content: Parenchyma is the most common type of ground tissue in plants. It is found in various parts of the plant, such as the cortex and pith of stems, the cortex of roots, the mesophyll of leaves, the pulp of fruits, and the endosperm of seeds. Parenchyma cells retain their meristematic ability, meaning they can divide even after they mature. These cells have thin, flexible cell walls and are generally cube-shaped and loosely packed. They contain large central vacuoles, which store nutrients and water. In leaves, parenchyma cells form the mesophyll and are responsible for photosynthesis and gas exchange. The shape and function of parenchyma cells vary depending on their location. For example, epidermal parenchyma cells in leaves are barrel-shaped and lack chloroplasts, serving as a protective barrier for internal tissues. In the spongy mesophyll of leaves, parenchyma cells are spherical, loosely arranged, and have large intercellular spaces, which, along with guard cells of stomata, create a system for gas exchange. Collenchyma tissue consists of elongated cells with unevenly thickened walls. These cells provide structural support, particularly in growing shoots and leaves. Collenchyma is exemplified by the resilient strands found in celery stalks. The thickness of collenchyma cell walls can increase by 40–100% in response to mechanical stress, such as wind. The name collenchyma is derived from the Greek word kolla, meaning glue, referring to the glistening appearance of the walls in fresh tissues. There are three main types of collenchyma: angular collenchyma (thickened at intercellular contact points), tangential collenchyma (cells arranged in rows with thickened tangential walls), and lacunar collenchyma (cells with intercellular spaces and thickening near these spaces). Sclerenchyma is a supporting tissue composed of two main types of cells: fibers and sclereids. These cells have walls made of cellulose and lignin. Sclerenchyma cells are typically dead at maturity and have extremely thick secondary walls, which can occupy up to 90% of the cell's volume. The term sclerenchyma comes from the Greek word skleros, meaning hard, reflecting the rigidity of these cells. Sclerenchyma fibers are economically significant as they are used to produce materials like flax, hemp, jute, and ramie for textiles. These fibers are long, slender cells that occur in bundles or strands and are known for their high tensile strength. Sclereids, another type of sclerenchyma cell, are shorter and more variable in shape. They can be isodiametric, elongated, forked, or branched. Sclereids are found in various plant parts, such as the gritty texture of pears and the hard cores of apples. They also form the shells of seeds and the stones of drupes like cherries and plums. The cell walls of sclereids are thick and layered, often with branched pits called ramiform pits. These cells provide structural support and protection in plants.
